name: Spinning Cosmic String
description: The spacetime around an infinitely thin, straight string that carries angular momentum as well as mass, flat everywhere off the string. The mass removes a wedge from every plane the string crosses, the spin shifts time by $8\pi GJ/c^4$ on each circuit of the string, and within $r = 4GJ/(c^3 - 4G\mu c)$ the circles around it are closed timelike curves.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The string has mass $\mu$ and angular momentum $J$ per unit length, which enter through $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$ and the length $a = 4GJ/c^3$.
history: Take one dimension of space away from Einstein's gravity and spacetime is flat wherever there is no matter, as Stanley Deser, Roman Jackiw, and Gerard 't Hooft found in 1984 [deser1984]. A source there affects the geometry only globally, through its mass and its angular momentum [deser1984]. The mass cuts a wedge of angle $8\pi G\mu/c^2$ out of the plane around the particle and leaves a cone [deser1992time]. The angular momentum does something stranger: in the coordinates that make the spacetime look flat, time jumps by $8\pi GJ/c^4$ on every trip around the particle [deser1992time]. Deser and Jackiw called this a "time-helical structure", a spiral staircase in time whose pitch is proportional to the spin [deser1992time].¶Nothing in that geometry changes if a third dimension of space runs along the particle, so the same solution is the field of an infinitely long, thin, straight string with mass $\mu$ and angular momentum $J$ per unit length [deser1992time, galtsov1993]. Cosmic strings could carry such spin: Pawel Mazur argued in 1986 that spinning strings occur naturally in spontaneously broken grand unified theories [mazur1986]. With the spin set to zero the solution is the Vilenkin-Gott cosmic string [soleng1992]. The metric with both parameters is the general time independent solution outside any cylindrically symmetric matter confined to a bounded region of the plane [deser1992time].¶Close to the string a circle at constant $t$, $r$, and $z$ is a closed timelike curve when $r < 4GJ/(c^3 - 4G\mu c)$: ride once around it and you come home at the event you left [deser1992time]. Deser, Jackiw, and 't Hooft saw these curves in 1984 and added that "such closed timelike contours are not possible in a space with n moving spinless particles, where angular momentum is purely orbital" [carroll1994]. The loophole was motion: two strings without spin, passing one another fast enough, do carry closed timelike curves, as J. Richard Gott found in 1991 [gott1991]. The pair's total momentum is that of a tachyon, the three replied in 1992 [deser1992]. An open universe whose total momentum is timelike has no room for such a pair, by the proof Sean Carroll, Edward Farhi, Alan Guth, and Ken Olum gave in 1994 [carroll1994]. As for the spinning string itself, intrinsic spin attached to a cosmic string "may still be deemed unphysical", in Deser and Jackiw's verdict, since its momentum density is built from derivatives of a delta function [deser1992time].¶A spinning string is the gravitational analogue of the solenoid of Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm, with $J$ in the role of the magnetic flux and the energy of a passing particle in the role of its charge [mazur1987]. Mazur argued in 1986 that a wave function single valued around the string has its energy quantised, $E = n\hbar c^4(1 - 4G\mu/c^2)/4GJ$ [mazur1986, mazur1987]. Joseph Samuel and Bala Iyer disputed the argument in 1987, and Mazur conceded in reply that nothing in the physics of the string forces the energies to be quantised [samuel1987, mazur1987]. He kept the condition as a postulate: at exactly those energies a particle scatters off the string as if it were not there, so the region of closed timelike curves goes undetected [mazur1987]. Send two particles around the string along the same closed path at the same speed in opposite directions and they come home $16\pi GJ/c^4$ apart, the one that raced against the spin arriving late, as Diego Harari and Alexios Polychronakos computed in 1988 [harari1988]. The Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations around the spinning particle have exact solutions, which Philipp de Sousa Gerbert and Jackiw found in 1989, noting obstacles to a consistent quantum mechanical interpretation of them [gerbert1989].¶A string with no thickness is a singular source: the spinning solution has torsion where the source sits, as de Sousa Gerbert showed in 1990 [gerbert1990]. Would a string with some thickness, made of ordinary matter, still make the curves? In Einstein-Cartan theory, where the gravitational effect of spin is torsion, Harald Soleng built one in 1992, a string with its spin polarised along its axis, matched to the spinning exterior [soleng1992, soleng1994]. General relativity seemed to say yes as well: the interiors Bjørn Jensen and Soleng derived in 1992 were reported to satisfy the weak and dominant energy conditions, some with closed timelike curves inside the string and outside it [jensen1992]. The answer turned to no in 1993, when Pietro Menotti and Domenico Seminara proved that a stationary, rotationally symmetric source obeying the weak energy condition, in an open universe with no closed timelike curves at spatial infinity, has no closed timelike curves anywhere [menotti1993]. Soleng reexamined both models in 1994 and found the flaw in each: where the curves exist, the Einstein-Cartan string has a spin energy density larger than its net energy density, and the strings without torsion carry a heat flow so large that the energy density is negative in some frames [soleng1994].¶Lifted to four dimensions in a boost covariant way, the spinning particle's metric becomes a chiral conical spacetime, which holds the spinning string as one case and Jacob Bekenstein's twisted string as another, as Dmitri Gal'tsov and Patricio Letelier showed in 1993 [galtsov1993]. Letelier described such strings in 1995 as a line of torsion along the string [letelier1995]. Could collapsing matter make the closed timelike curves? Filipe Mena, José Natário, and Paul Tod tried it in 2008 with a rotating cylindrical shell of null dust collapsing in flat space, the spinning string's metric outside it [mena2008]. The shell bounces before it reaches the radius at which closed timelike curves would form [mena2008].

related.text: The string with its spin switched off, $J = 0$. The helix in time closes up and only the cone is left [soleng1992].
The vacuum outside any straight rotating cylinder, curved off the axis. The flat one among Lewis's fields, $n = 1$ with $q = 0$, is the spinning string [bronnikov2020, jensen1992].
Flat spacetime with a wedge cut out along the string and the two faces glued back together a time $8\pi GJ/c^4$ out of step [deser1992time].

Two strings without spin whose closed timelike curves come from their motion. J. Richard Gott found them in 1991, seven years after Deser, Jackiw, and 't Hooft wrote that orbital angular momentum alone would not do it [gott1991, carroll1994].

A spinning cylinder of dust with closed timelike curves far from its axis. The spinning string keeps its closed timelike curves close in, within $r = 4GJ/(c^3 - 4G\mu c)$ [vanstockum1937, deser1992time].

The NUT parameter is a magnetic mass for gravity, and Charles Misner hid its string by making time periodic. Pawel Mazur drew the analogy in 1986: a wave around a spinning string is single valued only at quantised energies [misner1963, mazur1986].

The black hole of gravity in three dimensions, which needs a negative cosmological constant [banados1992]. Without one a spinning source is this string seen end on, and Neil Cornish and Norman Frankel found in 1994 that rotating matter there generally brings closed timelike curves or infinite shear [deser1984, cornish1994].
The straight string given a wave where this one is given spin. Its curvature scalars vanish as well, while the spacetime is curved wherever the wave passes [kaloper1997, anderson1999].

Soleng's thick string with $M = \Omega r^2/c$ and $\rho = r$ all the way out, a homogeneous universe of charged dust in rigid rotation. Its closed timelike curves lie outside $r = c/\Omega$, where the string's lie inside $r_c$ [soleng1994, som1968].

A slice across the string with the spin taken away. Deser, Jackiw, and 't Hooft met the spinning string as a spinning particle in three dimensions, in the paper that gives the cones of the particles without spin [deser1984].

coordinates.name: Proper Radius
domains: r < a/b \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, z \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Spin length, $a = 4GJ/c^3$, which sets the radius $r_c = a/b$, with $J$ the string's angular momentum per unit length; a circuit of the string shifts the flat time $t + a\phi/c$ by $2\pi a/c$
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use Deser and Jackiw's coordinates $(t, r, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ the proper distance from the string, $z$ the proper length along it, and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Rescaled Radius
domains: \rho < a \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, \rho, z \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Spin length, $a = 4GJ/c^3$, which sets the radius $r_c = a/b$, with $J$ the string's angular momentum per unit length; a circuit of the string shifts the flat time $t + a\phi/c$ by $2\pi a/c$
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$ of Cornish and Frankel and of Mena, Natário, and Tod, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, and $\rho = br$ for $r$ the proper distance from the string, so that the deficit sits in $g_{\rho\rho} = 1/b^2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Circumference Radius
domains: R = 0 \;\text{(the circle of constant } t, R, z \text{ is null)}

parameters.description: Spin length, $a = 4GJ/c^3$, which sets the radius $r_c = a/b$, with $J$ the string's angular momentum per unit length; a circuit of the string shifts the flat time $t + a\phi/c$ by $2\pi a/c$
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use Cornish and Frankel's coordinates $(t, R, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, and $R = \sqrt{b^2r^2 - a^2}$ for $r$ the proper distance from the string, so that the circle of constant $t$, $R$, and $z$ has circumference $2\pi R$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Helical Time

parameters.description: Spin length, $a = 4GJ/c^3$, which sets the radius $r_c = a/b$, with $J$ the string's angular momentum per unit length; a circuit of the string shifts the flat time $t + a\phi/c$ by $2\pi a/c$
$b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

coordinates.convention: We use Deser and Jackiw's flat coordinates $(\tau, r, \tilde\phi, z)$, with $\tau = t + a\phi/c$ carrying dimensions of time and $\tilde\phi = b\phi$, so that the line element is Minkowski's and a circuit of the string carries $(\tau, \tilde\phi)$ to $(\tau + 2\pi a/c, \tilde\phi + 2\pi b)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Extended Source
domains: M^2 > \rho^2 \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, z \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Twist function, a length, which vanishes on the axis and equals $a = 4GJ/c^3$ at the surface of the string and beyond it
Radius function, a length: $\rho$ grows as $r$ near the axis, and at the surface of the string $\partial_r\rho = b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$
Proper radius of the string's surface, where the source ends and the flat exterior begins

coordinates.convention: We use Soleng's coordinates $(t, r, \phi, z)$ inside a string of finite thickness, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ the proper distance from the axis, and $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, and we leave the lengths $M(r)$ and $\rho(r)$ free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
